newsitem.title: USA: Hong Kong test for U.S.-China ties.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong test for U.S.-China ties.

text.p: Hong Kong with its uncertain future has become a significant litmus test for U.S.-China relations.

"China's meeting its obligations toward Hong Kong will be a test of its willingness to participate responsibly in an international system based on law," Secretary of State Madeleine Albright wrote in Newsweek magazine this week.

"This test has significant implications not only for Hong Kong but for China's standing in the world and for prospects of improved U.S.-China relations," she said, noting that those relations have gone through a difficult period since Beijing's 1989 crackdown on pro-democracy forces in Tiananmen Square.

Underscoring this message, she will be in Hong Kong on June 30 when Beijing takes control of the British colony for the first time in 156 years. She will attend the handover ceremonies and expects to meet a number of key players including Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook and C.H. Tung, Hong Kong's first China-appointed chief executive.

As Beijing reassumes control, most U.S. concerns focus on whether China will allow enough political freedoms so vibrant Hong Kong can maintain its way of life. The U.S. view is that civil liberties and the rule of law are essential to maintaining Hong Kong's stability.

But as one U.S. official told Reuters, "We're worried that neither the authorities in Beijing nor Tung will be sufficiently sensitive to or understand the relationship between the non-economic aspects of Hong Kong -- retaining political institutions, freedom of speech and freedom of assembly -- and the economic aspects."

Tung, while a well-respected Hong Kong businessman who is "not a toady" for China, nevertheless seems to have a "conservative Chinese authoritarian streak in him (and is determined) to prevent chaos" in the territory, he added.
The big question, another official said, is whether, when push comes to shove, Tung stands up for Hong Kong on crucial issues such as freedom of the press and independent courts.

Beijing agreed with London in its 1984 Joint Declaration on Hong Kong to maintain the territory's unique character, including political and economic freedoms that are at odds with the communist system in place throughout the rest of China. This is the "one country, two systems" concept.

Despite reaffirmations of this commitment, many American analysts criticise what they perceive as China's rollbacks on democratic freedoms. The administration agrees the decision to replace an elected legislative council with a provisional legislature not chosen by voters raises serious concerns.

Officials are sympathetic to Chinese arguments that the last British governor of Hong Kong, Chris Patten, "went too far in changing the rules" and expanding democratic reforms in the territory beyond the 1984 Joint Declaration.
But they say China should have accepted British-imposed reforms and kept the legislative council to encourage confidence in Beijing and its intentions.
In Hong Kong, Albright will urge that the new legislature, whose installation she has decided to boycott, confine itself to narrow issues and that new elections be held quickly.
In addition to shared values, the United States has a huge financial stake in Hong Kong and its economic dynamism.

Some 1,100 U.S. firms based there employ 250,000 workers, 10 percent of Hong Kong's workforce. Hong Kong is the 13th largest U.S. trading partner with two-way trade of more than $24 billion. Some 36,000 Americans live and work in Hong Kong. And there are 60-80 port calls by U.S. Navy ships every year, which China agreed to continue.

Albright, and to a lesser extent President Bill Clinton, have expressed determination to use their bully pulpits to make clear what Washington expects of China in Hong Kong. Both have pressed hard for Congress to support trade benefits for China, arguing their cancellation would badly harm Hong Kong.
